content: Syphilis seropositivity among antenatal care (ANC) attendees can serve as a valuable model for estimating syphilis incidence in the general population. This is particularly useful in understanding trends and targeting interventions. The incidence of gonorrhea in males is considered an excellent early warning indicator of unprotected sexual activity. However, measuring gonorrhea incidence in females is more challenging due to the frequent asymptomatic nature of the infection in women, which complicates interpretation and surveillance. The rate of urethral discharge among adult males is a key indicator for sexually transmitted infections (STIs). This is measured by the number of reported cases of urethral discharge in adult males over the past 12 months. In countries lacking widespread STI diagnostic capabilities, this serves as an early warning measure for unprotected sexual activity among men. Congenital syphilis incidence is determined by the number of reported cases (including live births and stillbirths) within the past 12 months. Monitoring trends in congenital syphilis can provide insights into the effectiveness of programmatic interventions aimed at eliminating mother-to-child transmission (EMTCT) of syphilis. HIV testing services (HTS) must always be voluntary and adhere to the World Health Organization’s (WHO) 5 Cs: Consent, Confidentiality, Counselling, Correct test results, and Connection to prevention, care, and treatment. Coerced or mandatory testing is not acceptable and undermines ethical medical practices. The proportion of people living with HIV (PLHIV) who have been diagnosed is a critical metric. However, inappropriate implementation of provider-initiated testing and counselling (PITC) persists in many settings. In 2012, WHO recommended a review of national HIV testing services (HTS) policies to eliminate all forms of non-voluntary testing. Various HTS approaches can be employed to reach populations at the highest risk of HIV, such as pregnant or breastfeeding women, infants, adolescents, serodiscordant couples, key populations, tuberculosis (TB) patients, and other context-specific priority groups. Countries can tailor their HTS strategies based on epidemiological and social contexts, as well as available resources, to maximize coverage and uptake. Strategic information allows programs to align HTS with prevention, treatment, care, and support services. Disaggregating service statistics by HIV test result, service delivery point, or population subgroup can help set HTS targets and improve service delivery. HIV rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) have been available since the 1990s and have significantly expanded access to HTS in both facility and community settings. However, many countries still restrict their use to specific personnel, such as trained healthcare providers, excluding lay providers or nurses. The use of RDTs for same-day results has increased interest in point-of-care (POC) technologies, such as CD4 instruments, to streamline linkages between testing and HIV care. HIV self-testing (HIVST) is gaining traction, with several countries adopting policies to support it. HIVST allows individuals to collect a specimen, perform a test, and interpret the result privately. However, it is an initial screening tool and requires confirmatory testing for reactive results. Countries are encouraged to plan for monitoring and reporting on HIVST. Voluntary counselling and testing (VCT) is a client-initiated form of HIV testing, often provided at standalone clinics or integrated facilities. Provider-initiated testing and counselling (PITC) is routinely offered by healthcare providers as part of standard medical care, but only after obtaining informed consent. Community-based HIV testing services are conducted outside conventional health facilities, such as in homes, workplaces, schools, or mobile clinics, to increase accessibility. Couples and partner HIV testing services encourage mutual disclosure and support, while partner testing involves individuals bringing their sexual partners for voluntary testing. Mandatory HIV testing, conducted as a legal or institutional requirement, is not supported by public health principles and is prohibited in many countries. Quality assurance in HTS is critical, particularly in settings adopting WHO antiretroviral (ARV) guidelines recommending immediate ART initiation following a positive diagnosis. Retesting individuals with an HIV-positive diagnosis using a second specimen at the time of ART initiation is essential to rule out misdiagnosis. Monitoring and evaluation (M&E) of HTS should focus on measuring population outcomes, such as the proportion of PLHIV who know their status, rather than merely counting the number of tests performed. This aligns with the first 90 of the 90–90–90 global treatment targets. Adjusting for retesting in HTS coverage estimates is crucial, especially among populations at high ongoing risk for HIV infection. Efforts to scale up and decentralize HTS must ensure high-quality testing and accurate diagnoses. Retesting is recommended for individuals at ongoing risk, those with inconclusive results, and to verify HIV-positive diagnoses. Periodic retesting is particularly important in high-prevalence settings and among key populations.
